title: Plant-Health Diagnosis, Confirmation and Look-Alike Problems

content.overview: Symptoms such as chlorosis, wilting, lesions or stunting can arise from pathogens, pests, nutrition, roots or environment. Advanced plant-health work separates observation from causal diagnosis and uses confirmation proportional to the consequence of being wrong.

vocabulary.definition: Direct evidence of a causal organism or agent, such as visible fungal structures or a detected pest.
A different cause that produces a similar visible symptom pattern.
Additional evidence used to strengthen or reject a proposed diagnosis.

sections.title: Start with a problem statement, not a treatment
sections.body: Document affected tissue, distribution, onset, progression and environmental context before deciding what caused the problem.

sections.title: High-consequence diagnoses deserve stronger evidence
sections.body: Recurring disease, propagation-source risk or widespread crop loss may justify microscopy, laboratory testing or expert confirmation rather than visual diagnosis alone.

sections.title: Abiotic problems belong in the differential
sections.body: Nutrient deficiency research shows visual patterns can be imperfect indicators. Irrigation, root-zone, light and environment should remain plausible alternatives until evidence separates them.

workedExamples: Wilting with wet media may indicate root dysfunction rather than a need for more irrigation.
White foliar material should be examined for diagnostic structures before assuming every white patch is powdery mildew.
commonMistakes: Choosing a product before identifying the problem.
Treating a symptom name as a causal diagnosis.
content.practicalApplication: For a significant plant-health event, write at least three plausible causes and one observation or test that would increase or decrease confidence in each before selecting a response.
content.summary: Diagnosis is an evidence process. Strong IPM decisions reduce uncertainty before adding interventions.
